title: Microscopic dynamics of contagion using active Brownian particles: universal scaling and propagation controlled by protection
abstract: Understanding how individual protection and population density influence epidemic spreading remains a central challenge in epidemiology. While classical compartmental models successfully describe the temporal evolution of epidemics, they do not explicitly account for the microscopic motion and spatial organisation of individuals. Here, we investigate contagion dynamics using an agent-based model of Active Brownian Particles (ABPs), where self-propelled agents interact through local contact and a prescribed fraction of the population is protected. By systematically varying the protected-agent fraction and the population density, we identify two distinct contagion regimes separated by a crossover protection of approximately $30\%$. Below this threshold, the maximum contagion rate follows the universal scaling $ν_{\mathrm{max}}\proptoφ^{1/2}$, indicating that disease transmission is governed primarily by frequency of encounters. Above the threshold, universal scaling is lost and protection becomes the dominant mechanism controlling epidemic spreading, with the strongest suppression occurring in low-density populations. These results demonstrate that microscopic active-matter models provide a powerful framework for investigating epidemic dynamics beyond the assumptions of well-mixed population models and reveal how spatial organisation and individual protection jointly determine contagion dynamics.
summary: This paper models disease spread using active matter particles to capture spatial effects missed by traditional epidemic models. It finds a critical protection threshold ($\approx 30\%$) that dictates whether contagion is governed by simple encounter frequency or by the protective mechanisms of the population. The work demonstrates the power of microscopic active-matter simulations for complex non-equilibrium dynamics.
main_problem: The study investigates how individual protection levels and population density influence the dynamics of epidemic spreading, moving beyond the limitations of classical well-mixed models.
main_result:
The contagion dynamics exhibit two distinct regimes separated by a crossover protection level ($\approx 30\%$): below this, scaling is universal ($
u_{max} \propto \phi^{1/2}$), while above it, protection becomes the dominant control mechanism.
method: The research employs an agent-based simulation model using Active Brownian Particles (ABPs) to simulate the spatial spread of infection.
model_or_system: The system models contagion using ABPs (S, I, P) interacting via a WCA potential in a 2D domain. The dynamics are governed by Langevin equations in the overdamped limit.
key_observables:
Maximum contagion rate ($
u_{max}$), normalized contagion rate ($I'(	au)/S_0$), and the time to peak contagion ($	au_{max}$).
important_parameters: Protected-agent fraction ($\chi$), population density (packing fraction $\phi$), and the crossover threshold ($\approx 0.3$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the overdamped limit approximation and assumes interactions are governed by the WCA potential.
figures_summary:
Figures illustrate the time evolution of infected agents ($I(	au)$) and the normalized maximum contagion rate ($
u_{max}\phi^{-1/2}$) as a function of the protected fraction ($\chi$) for various densities ($\phi$), clearly showing the crossover.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of classical models, then detailing the ABP framework, and finally analyzing the scaling behavior of the contagion rate across different protection and density regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on epidemiology, the use of active matter models (ABPs) to study non-equilibrium collective dynamics, phase transitions (the crossover), and universal scaling laws in a spatially structured system is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
